capabilities.target: Shell commands on the CI runner, full OS access, with the agent's environment (including GITHUB_TOKEN)
Workspace filesystem, including repository files and the .agent/ directory
.agent/config.yaml, the agent's own runtime configuration (model, autonomy, max_steps, tools, network)
Remote GitHub repository branch, reachable org-wide via a repo+workflow scoped PAT
A planned Slack workspace channel via a future Slack MCP server

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body, public repository, opened by any GitHub user via an issue template that applies the 'bug' label
Repository file contents read during reproduction and testing

instructions.note: "Pick up any issue labeled 'bug' and fix it end to end" grants open-ended authority over arbitrary future issues with no limit on which repos, file types, or changes are permissible.

The only control against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a prompt instruction, a behavioral, model-dependent control, with no structural enforcement such as an egress allowlist or scoped credential.

Line 5 says to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code, but line 6 gives the agent standing authority to modify its own config 'if you need extra tools'; the judgment of need is itself formed by reading the untrusted issue, so injected content can steer self-configuration without the model ever 'following an embedded instruction' in a way line 5 would catch.
The agent is given standing authority to alter its own runtime configuration with no approval gate, enabling persistent self-escalation (TC3).
autonomy: full and max_steps: null set no bound on unattended operation.

elements.name: Any GitHub user able to open issues
All org repositories reachable via the broad PAT

controls.name: Prompt rule: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply; a more capable or injected model can rationalize exceptions or split a forbidden action into steps that each look benign.

controls.name: Prompt rule: ignore instructions inside issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: A spotlighting-style instruction that only works if the model reliably distinguishes data from instructions; adaptive prompt injection routinely defeats this, and a more capable model follows longer, more convincing injected goals.

controls.name: Human pull request review before merge
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by human merge action outside the model; however it gates merge, not the push itself, and does not cover code that executes via push-triggered GitHub Actions workflows before any merge occurs.

controls.name: Repo-scoped, least-privilege token minted per task
controls.decay_rationale: Does not decay: the agent cannot use access it does not have.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for the CI sandbox
controls.decay_rationale: Blocks exfiltration destinations outside the allowlist regardless of model behavior, provided the allowlist excludes attacker-writable endpoints.

controls.name: Read-only mount for .agent/config.yaml with approval-gated changes
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the filesystem/orchestration layer; removes the model's ability to self-modify regardless of capability.

controls.name: Per-repo scoped push token without workflow permission
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped to one repo without workflow-write permission makes cross-repo and CI-workflow sinks unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Per-task step count, runtime, and spend ceiling
controls.decay_rationale: Hard ceiling enforced by the orchestrator; bounds runaway loops and cost regardless of model capability, though low-and-slow abuse within the cap still occurs.

controls.name: Tamper-evident, append-only action log
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by writing to a store the agent cannot modify; does not prevent actions but restores attributability.

controls.name: Provenance tagging on repository file writes
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the store if tags are written by the orchestrator rather than the model; a model-written tag would instead be dependent.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta variant: injected shell execution with org-wide credential and unrestricted egress (TC1/TC2)

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can author issue content that the agent reads and acts on.
Agent runs 'whatever commands it needs' to reproduce/test, with full environment access (including GITHUB_TOKEN) and unrestricted outbound network.

forecast.watch_signal: config.yaml's model field changes, or the model provider releases a new version while 'model: latest' auto-updates with no review (subject.model.swappable is true).

evidence.observation: tools include shell.run; GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope across all org repos; network is unrestricted.
'Run whatever commands you need to reproduce and test' directs shell execution based on the agent's reading of the issue, with no command allowlist.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the triggering content untrusted.

recommendations.action: Replace the org-wide PAT with a short-lived, repo-scoped token minted per task with no workflow scope.
Restrict the CI sandbox's outbound network to an allowlist of required package/registry endpoints; deny arbitrary destinations.
Run shell commands in an isolated sandbox where secrets are injected through a broker that redacts them from process environment and command output.
Log every shell command and outbound network call with alerting on unknown destinations.

findings.title: Self-modifying configuration driven by injected issue content (TC3)

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue content shapes what the model believes it 'needs'.
Prompt explicitly permits editing .agent/config.yaml 'if you need extra tools,' with no approval gate.

forecast.watch_signal: Repeated or unusual tool-list changes appearing in .agent/config.yaml commit history, or the model is swapped without review.

evidence.observation: 'You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task' grants standing self-modification authority with no approval step.
config.yaml sets model, autonomy, max_steps, tools, and network — all attacker-reachable targets of a self-config edit.

recommendations.action: Mount .agent/config.yaml read-only at runtime; route any legitimate tool/config change through a separate, human-approved CI job.
Remove the standing instruction granting self-config authority; require an explicit, out-of-band request for new tools instead.

findings.title: Confused deputy push with org-wide, workflow-scoped credential (TC4)

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue drives the end-to-end fix-and-push workflow.
Push executes with a PAT scoped to repo+workflow across all org repos, far broader than the single task repo.

findings.residual_rationale: The credited PR-review gate (control.pr_review_gate) only gates merge, not push; because the token carries workflow scope, a pushed branch can modify .github/workflows files that execute automatically on push, bypassing human review entirely. The credit math alone (step 2 unknown-volume gate plus step 4 behavioral discount) would float to moderate; this undetected bypass path keeps residual at high.

forecast.watch_signal: PAT scope widened further, branch protection disabled on any org repo, or workflow files modified by agent-pushed branches auto-executing before merge.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo + workflow scope on all org repos, far broader than the single repository the agent is meant to work in.
'Push a branch and open a PR when tests pass' executes github.push_branch using that broad credential, driven by an untrusted issue.

recommendations.action: Scope the push token to the single repository under task, with no workflow-write permission.
Require human review of the full diff (not a PR summary) before merge, and disable workflow execution on untrusted/unreviewed branches.
Alert when a pushed branch modifies files under .github/workflows/.

findings.title: No step, runtime, or spend bound on fully autonomous operation (ASI08)

forecast.watch_signal: CI runner cost or runtime per agent run rises, or the queue depth of 'bug'-labeled issues spikes.

evidence.observation: autonomy: full and max_steps: null set no bound on unattended operation.
Runs on a shared CI runner with outbound internet and no stated concurrency or cost limit; any issue labeled 'bug' can trigger a run.

recommendations.action: Set max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes in config.yaml, and add a per-run spend/cost ceiling.
Rate-limit concurrent issue-fixer runs per repository and add a cooldown between runs triggered by the same label.

findings.title: No tamper-evident action provenance for configure, push, or execute actions (ASI09/ASI10)

forecast.watch_signal: Absence of per-action audit log entries tied to a human-reviewable identity, surfaced during any security review or incident.

evidence.observation: No artifact describes an audit log, action provenance store, or any mechanism attributing agent actions to the triggering issue or a reviewable record.

recommendations.action: Write an append-only, tamper-evident log of every tool invocation, argument set, and resulting diff, correlated to the triggering issue id, stored outside the agent's write access.

findings.title: Repository content poisoning via injected-issue-driven writes (memory/trust laundering, TC5)

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue shapes what the agent writes during its fix.
Agent writes to arbitrary workspace/repository files with no path scope restriction.
Written content persists in the repository.
Future runs read this content and treat it as internal/trusted.
Content is pushed/branched before independent review completes.

findings.residual_rationale: The same workflow-scope bypass described for F3 applies here: a poisoned write can reach execution via a push-triggered workflow before any PR is reviewed or merged, so the credit the PR-review gate would otherwise earn is not available for this path. Residual is kept at high rather than the moderate the stacked credits would produce.

forecast.watch_signal: Workflow files modified by agent-authored commits, or branch protection/required review disabled.

evidence.observation: The agent reads an issue, writes a fix, and pushes/opens a PR in the same untrusted-triggered run, so content shaped by the issue can enter repository files before independent review occurs at push time.
fs.write has no stated path scope restriction excluding .agent/ or any directory, so the same run can modify arbitrary repository files.

recommendations.action: Tag file writes with provenance (triggering issue id, model version) at the storage layer and surface it prominently in the PR diff for reviewer attention.
Disable workflow execution on branches pushed by the agent until after human-approved merge.

findings.title: Planned Slack MCP server combined with existing self-config authority opens a new unmonitored egress channel

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue content could describe a 'need' for Slack notification.
Agent already has standing authority to add tools to its own config.
Once the planned Slack MCP server exists, the agent could add it to its own tool list and use it to send data externally with no additional review.

forecast.watch_signal: Slack MCP server entries appended to .agent/config.yaml's tools list, or a new MCP client config referencing a Slack server.

evidence.observation: 'The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter' describes a planned capability not yet built.
Existing standing self-config authority would let the agent add the future Slack tool to its own tool list once available, without a new review.

recommendations.action: When the Slack MCP server is added, pin its tool definitions, scope its credentials to a single channel, and apply the same read-only config mount so the agent cannot wire itself up to it unsupervised.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent runs as a single first-party process with no peer agents or servers authenticating as issue-fixer; there is no identity of this process that could be spoofed toward another party in this design.
This flow carries content inbound from a GitHub issue to the agent and does not itself move data out of the trust boundary; outbound disclosure is covered at flow.shell_egress and flow.git_push.
The artifacts do not state whether GitHub account verification (email, phone, account age) is required before an account can open issues and apply the bug label.
This flow carries content already resident inside the trust domain to the agent process; tampering with the underlying content is addressed at store.repo_store rather than at this read path.
Flow is inbound only to the agent and does not cross the trust boundary; disclosure risk from repository content is addressed at store.repo_store and at the egress flows.
Reading repository files is a bounded, synchronous operation; broader availability risk from unattended operation is covered under finding F4 at the process level.
The config file references the credential only through an environment variable name, not its value; disclosure of the credential itself is addressed at cap.shell and flow.shell_egress.
The artifacts do not state whether the repository contains any sensitive data beyond source code, so disclosure sensitivity of this store cannot be fully assessed.
A file store for source code is not identified in the artifacts as a rate-limited or capacity-constrained resource relevant to an availability attack.
This element represents the set of destination repositories reachable via the broad token; it is a destination, not a source whose identity could be spoofed toward the agent.
The Slack MCP server integration is only described as a future plan; no authentication method has been specified for assessment.
Same planned-feature gap; no detail exists on how actions through a future Slack integration would be attributed.
Slack MCP server integration is planned, not yet specified; no design detail exists to assess tampering risk on this future flow.
Same planned-feature gap; data sensitivity and payload content for a future Slack channel are not yet defined.
Planned integration with no rate-limiting or volume details available for assessment.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted GitHub issue (any user, public repo) reaches an unattended execute capability holding an org-wide, workflow-scoped credential and unrestricted network egress, a configure capability with standing self-modification authority, and a push capability whose token reaches every org repository. Residual sits at high rather than lower: the design's only structural control, PR review before merge, is credited by the rubric but its real coverage is undermined by the token's workflow scope, which lets a pushed branch execute CI workflows before any human review (stated in residual_rationale on F3 and F6); the remaining credit comes from two behavioral, model-dependent prompt rules (control.never_delete_exfiltrate, control.ignore_embedded_instructions), which the floor caps at one tier of credit. Forecast rises back to critical because control.ignore_embedded_instructions is the single control credited across nearly every finding, and it is dependent: a model upgrade or a longer task horizon is expected to defeat it across F1, F2, F3, and F6 simultaneously, and the planned Slack MCP server (F7) would hand the agent, via its existing self-config authority, a brand-new unmonitored egress channel with no additional review required. Two STRIDE coverage pairs are recorded not_applicable beyond the simple default (store.repo_store/denial_of_service, ext.github_org/spoofing); both are justified in-line as structural non-fits rather than unexamined gaps.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior, which was not provided.

No tool manifest or MCP server definitions were provided beyond the tools list in config.yaml, so capability scope beyond shell/fs/git is inferred; confidence on cross-tool chaining is medium to high depending on the path.

Whether a GitHub branch protection rule actually requires human review of the full diff before merge is not explicitly stated; the existence of a PR-based review gate is inferred from 'open a PR when tests pass' and is treated as declared, not verified.
The Slack MCP server integration is described only as a future plan with no configuration detail; findings referencing it (F7) are forecast-only and low confidence.
